clue.text: University exams for Alfred and Peter?

definitions.meaning: at Oxford the final classics examinations go by this nickname
King Alfred and Tsar Peter each carry the epithet 'the Great', so together they are a pair of such figures

explanation.walkthrough: Greats is the Oxford name for the honours course and exams in classics (Literae Humaniores).
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford's classics finals are nicknamed this, and Alfred and Peter are both monarchs styled 'the Great'.

clue.text: I would be the last to bring this up

definitions.text: I would be the last to bring this up

parts.words: I would be the last to bring this up
parts.note: the speaker who is last in a procession is said to bring up the back of it, the idiom behind the clue

explanation.surface: Someone protests they would never raise an awkward subject.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring up the rear is to come last, so the back position is what the last person brings up.

clue.text: In which somebody is travelling flat out?

definitions.text: In which somebody is travelling flat out?

parts.words: In which somebody is travelling flat out?
parts.note: flat out reads as at top speed, but the patient is lying flat on a stretcher in an emergency vehicle

explanation.surface: A question about some vehicle going at full speed.
explanation.definitionFit: An emergency vehicle carries a patient lying down, often at high speed with sirens.

clue.text: Fly Spitfire by day

parts.note: a spitfire is a fiery, quarrelsome woman, a shrew

explanation.surface: An instruction to pilot a Spitfire fighter plane in daylight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' and 'Spitfire' suggest the wartime aircraft; here Spitfire is a hot-tempered woman and Fly is the slang adjective for sharp or knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Fly is British slang for knowing and astute, a synonym of being sharp-witted.

clue.text: Bill takes detectives to hospital department after crash

parts.note: AC, short for account, is a bill
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's detectives
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill brings police officers to a hospital ward after a road smash.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name but gives AC, the abbreviation for account.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash is a mishap or collision, a synonym for an unplanned mishap on the road.

clue.text: One can judge for oneself when it is reached

definitions.text: One can judge for oneself when it is reached

parts.words: One can judge for oneself when it is reached
parts.note: describes the point in life at which a young person is deemed able to make responsible decisions alone

explanation.surface: A remark about a stage after which people may trust their own judgement.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase names the legal or social stage at which a person may decide matters for themselves.

clue.text: Working-class symbol worn by the clergy?

definitions.meaning: a flat woollen cap is the stereotypical headgear of a British working man
the clergy are known as the cloth, so their headgear would be a cap of the cloth

explanation.definitionFit: The flat cap is a British emblem of the working man, and 'the cloth' is a nickname for clergy.

clue.text: A bit of exercise?

definitions.meaning: a boring tool's cutting piece, the bit fitted in a power tool
repeated military or practice routine, as in fire practice

explanation.definitionFit: A boring bit is called a drill, and so is a repetitive training exercise for soldiers.

clue.text: Sensible number join production of Lear

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote the Book of Nonsense, so his output is nonsense verse

explanation.surface: A level-headed actor joins a staging of King Lear.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear suggests Shakespeare's king, but it is Edward Lear, the Victorian writer of nonsense verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-nonsense approach is practical and down-to-earth, hence sensible.

clue.text: Drunk, a mob jeer a troopers' rally

indicators.note: being drunk suggests these letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunken crowd heckles a gathering of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: Troopers here are Scouts, whose large international gathering is a jamboree.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamboree is a large gathering of Scouts, who are organised in troops.

clue.text: Experts know them to be edible bulbs

definitions.meaning: the idiom says an expert 'knows their ...', meaning knows the subject thoroughly
pungent vegetables grown as bulbs and used in cooking

explanation.definitionFit: Knowing one's onions is an idiom for expertise, and the onion is an edible bulb vegetable.

clue.text: Rule not mainly enforced?

parts.note: not mainly is read as not of the main, the sea, so the rule belongs on dry ground instead

explanation.surface: A complaint about a regulation that is seldom applied.
explanation.definitionFit: The established legal system of a country, as opposed to maritime law of the main or sea.

clue.text: Official in Foreign Office about to divulge secrets

parts.note: bureau is the French word for office, so a foreign office
C is short for circa, about
to rat is to inform or betray secrets

explanation.surface: A diplomat in Whitehall is poised to leak confidential material.
explanation.walkthrough: Foreign Office looks like the British ministry; it means an office in a foreign language, French bureau.
explanation.definitionFit: A bureaucrat is an administrative official, typically in government.

clue.text: Game at home results in defeat

parts.note: RU is rugby union
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A home fixture ends in a loss.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin is downfall or utter defeat, a synonym of collapse.

clue.text: Fancies a drink when in semi-retirement

indicators.note: in places the drink inside the other piece
retirement means going back, so the word semi is read backwards

parts.note: gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone half retired enjoys a tipple now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen hides the split: 'semi' is fodder and 'retirement' the reversal signal, giving IMES; 'in' then holds the drink inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something is to suppose or picture it, a synonym of conceiving it in the mind.

clue.text: One is well rid of it

definitions.text: One is well rid of it

parts.words: One is well rid of it
parts.note: the idiom 'well rid of' is read literally: getting rid of this makes one healthy

explanation.surface: A remark that someone is better off without something.
explanation.definitionFit: Poor bodily condition, sickness; losing it leaves one well.

clue.text: Its members are outnumbered

parts.note: describes a group smaller than the rest, whose members are always fewer

explanation.surface: A remark about a club whose members are heavily outnumbered.
explanation.definitionFit: A smaller group within a population, by definition fewer than the larger part.

clue.text: Vegetable stew for Eric and Alec

indicators.note: to stew is to cook ingredients together, so the two names' letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cooks a vegetable stew for two friends.
explanation.definitionFit: A root vegetable, a variety of celery grown for its knobbly edible root.

clue.text: No idea where you are? Behold the way!

parts.note: lo is an old word for behold
ST, for street, is a way

explanation.surface: A bewildered traveller is shown the path to take.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unable to tell where you are means being astray, without bearings.

clue.text: Seat is free for the rest of the afternoon

indicators.note: set free, the letters break loose and rearrange

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chair is available so someone can relax for the remainder of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is an afternoon nap or rest, taken in hot countries.

clue.text: Reserve added to a team

parts.note: put on means added, as in putting on weight
a team is one side

explanation.surface: A substitute player joins the squad.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something aside is to save it for later, a synonym of keeping it back.

clue.text: Ring a poor actor up in America

parts.note: O is ring-shaped

indicators.note: in a down clue up means these pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a ham is a bad, overacting actor

explanation.surface: Someone phones an unsuccessful actor in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns A HAM into MAHA, placed after O. The definition is loose: the answer is a city in America (Nebraska).
explanation.definitionFit: Omaha is a city found in America, in the state of Nebraska.

clue.text: Old students burden of debt?

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students

explanation.surface: Former undergraduates weighed down by loans.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUS is the UK's National Union of Students; the question mark marks the debt as just one kind of burden.
explanation.definitionFit: Onus is a burden or responsibility, here the obligation to repay what is owed.

clue.text: Marian in fashion — wearing this designer label?

indicators.note: fashion as a verb means shape, so the name is remade

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman named Marian is stylishly dressed in a famous brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Armani is an Italian fashion house, a designer label of clothing.

clue.text: Saucy book going to part of Oxford?

indicators.note: going to means the book is attached at the end

parts.note: an Oxford is a style of lace-up shoe, and its inner sole is part of it
NT is the New Testament, a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A cheeky novel heads for a corner of the university city.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford suggests the city or university; it is a lace-up shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Saucy means cheeky or impudent, a synonym of rudely disrespectful.

clue.text: A way to take one day off and calm down

parts.note: ST, for street, is a way

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to take a day's holiday to relax.
explanation.definitionFit: This interjection is said to urge someone to calm down or be careful.

clue.text: Horrified at being cut by jagged gash

indicators.note: cut by means the other piece goes into the gap made in this one
jagged means torn and irregular, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is appalled at being wounded by a ragged cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'at' as part of 'horrified at', but it is the word being cut; 'jagged' scrambles gash, and 'being cut by' puts that scramble into the little word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means struck with horror, filled with shock and dismay.
